d.g: A straight line which a curve approaches arbitrarily closely as it goes to infinity. The limit of the curve; its tangent "at infinity".
Anything which comes near to but never meets something else.
d.x: Language, in relation to thought, must ever be regarded as an asymptote.

d.g: To approach, but never quite touch, a straight line, as something goes to infinity.
d.x:
2006: Neil deGrasse Tyson, The Perimeter of Ignorance
As you become more scientific, yes, the religiosity drops off, but it asymptotes.

asymptote.e: circa 1650, from Ancient Greek ἀσύμπτωτη (asúmptōtē), the feminine of Apollonius Pergaeus' (circa 200 BC) Ancient Greek adjective ἀσύμπτωτος (asúmptōtos, “not falling together”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + συν- (sun-, “together”) + πτωτός (ptōtós, “fallen”). See also a-, syn-, -ote.

d.g: Synonym of asynchrony.
The state of being asynchronous, or out of synchronization
The position of a baby in the uterus such that the head is presenting first, tilted to the shoulder and thus no longer in line with the birth canal.
Omission of conjunctions, especially for rhetorical effect.
d.x: Asyndeton, or the Loose language... as thus. I saw it, I said it, I will sweare it.

asyndeton.e: From Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-, non-”) and the neuter substantive of σῠ́νδετος (sŭ́ndetos, “bound, joined”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). Equivalent to a- + syndeton.

d.g: A lack of muscular coordination
defective or absent coordination between organs, muscles, limbs or joints, resulting in a loss in movement or speed
An absence of a systole; a failure of the heart to contract.

asystole.e: English a- English systole English asystole From a- + systole.

d.g: To move upward, to fly, to soar.
d.x: He ascended to heaven upon a cloud.

d.g: To slope in an upward direction.
To go up.
d.x: You ascend the stairs and take a right.

d.g: To succeed a ruler on (the throne).
d.x: She ascended the throne when her mother abdicated.

ascend.e: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.

d.g: To find out definitely; to discover or establish.
d.x: As soon as we ascertain what the situation is, we can plan how to proceed.

d.g: To look for something lost.

ascertain.e: From Middle English acerteynen, from Old French acertener, from a- (“to, towards”) + certener (“make sure of”), from the adjective certain, from Latin certus (“certain, fixed”). Compare to Spanish acertar.

d.g: To regard as arising from a specified cause or source.
d.x: One may ascribe these problems to the federal government; however, at this stage it is unclear what caused them.

d.g: To attribute (a book, painting, or any other work of art or literature) to a writer or creator.
d.x: It is arguable as to whether we can truly ascribe this play to Shakespeare.

d.g: To believe in or agree with; to subscribe.

d.g: To overcome or successfully argue against; defeat.

d.g: To murder someone, especially an important person, by a sudden or obscure attack, especially for ideological or political reasons.
To harm, ruin, or defame severely or destroy by treachery, slander, libel, or obscure attack.

d.g: To determine, estimate or judge the value of; to evaluate; to estimate.
d.x: He assessed the situation.

d.g: To impose or charge, especially as punishment for an infraction.

d.g: To change into or pronounce with the accompaniment of a sibilant sound or sounds.
To change by assibilation.

assonate.e: From Latin assonō, from ad (“to, towards”) + sonō (“to sound, resound”).

d.x: They appear […] no way assorted to those with whom they must associate.

d.g: To be of a kind with, to harmonise or match.
To be associated with; to consort with.
To furnish with, or make up of, various sorts or a variety of goods.
d.x: to assort a cargo

d.g: To lessen the intensity of, to mitigate or relieve (hunger, emotion, pain, etc.).
d.x: Refreshing winds the summer's heat assuage.

d.g: To pacify or soothe (someone).

assuage.e: From Middle English aswagen, from Old French asuagier (“to appease, to calm”), from Vulgar Latin *assuāviō (“to sweeten, to butter up, to calm”), derived from Latin ad- + suāvis (“sweet”) + -iō.

d.g: To authenticate by means of belief; to surmise; to suppose to be true, especially without proof.
d.x: We assume that, as her parents were dentists, she knows quite a bit about dentistry.

d.g: To take on a position, duty or form.
d.x: Mr. Jones will assume the position of a lifeguard until a proper replacement is found.

d.g: To adopt a feigned quality or manner; to claim without right; to arrogate.
d.x: He assumed an air of indifference.

d.g: To receive, adopt (a person).
d.x: The sixth was a young knight of lesser renown and lower rank, assumed into that honorable company.

assume.e: From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sūmō (“take up, assume”).

d.g: To make sure and secure; ensure.
To give (someone) confidence in the trustworthiness of (something).
d.x: I assure you that the program will work smoothly when we demonstrate it to the client.

d.g: To reassure.

assure.e: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer), from Latin ad- + securus (“secure”). Cognate with Spanish asegurar. Doublet of assecure.

d.g: To surprise greatly.
